subject: Culture
title: Arranged Marriage
description: A quick, practical guide to Arranged Marriage.

hook.text: Over half the world's marriages are arranged by families. In the West, the idea sounds controlling.

buildup.text: Arranged marriages prioritize compatibility, family bonds, and economic stability over romantic love.

discovery.text: Studies show arranged marriages report equal or higher satisfaction than love marriages over time.

twist.text: Forced marriage and arranged marriage are not the same. Consent is present in one and absent in the other.

climax.text: Western culture romanticizes choice. Eastern culture trusts experience. Both produce love—just on different timelines.

punchline.text: Love at first sight or love at first year—both work.

quiz.question: How do satisfaction rates compare between arranged and love marriages?
options: Arranged marriages report equal or higher satisfaction

details.summary: Arranged marriage — where families select partners rather than individuals choosing for themselves — remains the norm for millions worldwide, particularly in South Asia, the Middle East, and parts of Africa. Far from forced marriage, many arranged unions involve significant input from the couple.
details.whyItMatters: Arranged marriage challenges Western romantic assumptions. Understanding the spectrum from collaborative family matchmaking to coerced unions prevents oversimplification of a practice affecting billions.
takeaways: Arranged marriages account for over 50% of marriages globally
Modern arranged marriages often involve the couple's consent and input
Arranged marriage is distinct from forced marriage, which lacks consent

faq.question: What is the difference between arranged and forced marriage?
faq.answer: In arranged marriage, families introduce compatible partners and the couple can accept or reject the match. In forced marriage, one or both parties have no genuine choice.

faq.question: Do arranged marriages have higher divorce rates?
faq.answer: Generally no — arranged marriage divorce rates are significantly lower than love marriages in most studies. However, this partly reflects cultural pressures against divorce rather than higher satisfaction.
